Rembrandt's Self-Portrait with Two Circles, painted in 1665 near the end of his life, shows the aging artist standing before a canvas bearing two concentric circles, a symbol of perfect geometry and artistic aspiration. This is a meditation on mastery, mortality, and the artist's enduring pursuit of transcendent form amid personal hardship.

Rembrandt paints himself at the easel, palette and brush in hand, gazing outward with dignified, almost defiant composure. His face is heavily shadowed and his clothing is plain and worn, belying his eminence—a reflection of his personal decline into financial difficulty in his later years. The two circles on the canvas behind him have invited allegorical interpretation as perfect geometric forms, the limits of human achievement, or the divine aspiration that drives creation. Some scholars suggest they represent the earth and heaven, the material and ideal, or simply the artist's solitary creative labour.

The painting measures approximately 114 by 94 centimetres and is housed in the Iveagh Bequest at Kenwood House in London. Rembrandt executed over one hundred self-portraits across his lifetime—a unique commitment to the form that tracks his artistic evolution and personal aging—making this final introspective work a late-career meditation on art and mortality.
